title: Chunking to remember
keyIdea: Your memory can only hold a few pieces at a time, about four. Chunking means grouping lots of small things into a few bigger pieces, so there is less to hold. A long number like 358294716 is 9 pieces, but 358 294 716 is only 3. A shopping list is easier as 3 groups (fruit, bath time, breakfast) than as 9 separate things. A long word is easier to spell in beats (yes-ter-day). Chunks that mean something, like real words, are the easiest of all.
familyTip: Next time you give your child a phone number or a door code, say it in chunks with a pause: 0 7 7, pause, 1 2 3, pause, 4 5 6. Before a trip to the shop, ask them to sort the list into groups out loud. Ask: how many groups do we need to remember?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: pour 9 numbers into a small memory, break them into chunks that fit, sort a shopping list, and split words into chunks.

kid: Your memory can only hold a few things at once. Try to hold 9 numbers one by one, and some fall out.
A chunk is a group. Put the numbers into groups of 3: 358, then 294, then 716. Now there are only 3 pieces to hold, and they fit.
You can chunk a list too. Put the things into groups, like fruit, bath time and breakfast. Then you remember 3 groups, and each group helps you think of what is in it.
Long words are easier to spell in chunks. Clap the beats: yes, ter, day. Learn one chunk at a time. Chunks that mean something, like cat, dog and hen, are the easiest to remember.
adult: Ages 6 to 7. Chunking is one of the memory strategies in the EEF's guidance on metacognition and self-regulated learning: children learn a named strategy, see it modelled, then choose it themselves. It also matches how we teach spelling by syllables and teach phone numbers in groups. Key words: memory, remember, chunk, group, piece, pattern.

The idea behind it: working memory holds only a few chunks at once, about four for adults (Cowan, 2001), and fewer for young children. Miller's famous 'seven, plus or minus two' (1956) is now thought too high. A chunk can be big if it means something, so 'cat' is one chunk, while c-a-t is three.

Common mistakes: thinking saying a list faster helps (it is still the same number of pieces); making one giant chunk (it is too big to hold); leaving single leftovers that become extra pieces; breaking words in places that do not match the beats; and making chunks that mean nothing. Careful chunking makes groups of 2 to 4 that hang together.

In the lab your child pours 9 numbers into a memory box with 4 spaces and sees 5 fall out, breaks the number into chunks until it fits, sorts 9 shopping things into 3 baskets, splits yesterday into its beats, and finds 3 animal words hidden in a row of letters.

practice.prompt: Which is the easiest way to remember the number 482613?
practice.hint: Fewer pieces are easier to hold.
practice.explain: 482 613 is just 2 pieces to remember. One at a time is 6 pieces.

practice.prompt: A list has {g} groups with {k} things in each group. How many things are on the list?
practice.hint: Count {k} things for each of the {g} groups.
practice.explain: {g} groups of {k} is {=g*k} things, but you only need to remember {g} groups.

practice.prompt: How would you chunk the word butterfly to spell it?
practice.hint: Clap the beats as you say it slowly.
practice.explain: Butterfly has 3 beats: but, ter, fly. Spell one chunk at a time.

practice.prompt: A door code is split into {c} chunks with {k} digits in each chunk. How many digits is the whole code?
practice.hint: Count {k} digits for each of the {c} chunks.
practice.explain: {c} chunks of {k} digits is {=c*k} digits, but you only hold {c} chunks in your memory.

practice.prompt: Why do chunks help you remember?
choices: There are fewer pieces to hold
practice.hint: Think about the memory box in the lab.
practice.explain: Your memory holds only a few pieces. Chunks turn lots of pieces into a few.

choices: A small group of things you remember as one piece
pool.explain: A chunk is a small group, like 358, that you hold as one piece.

pool.prompt: You need to buy apples, soap, bread, pears, shampoo and milk. What helps most?
choices: Group them: fruit, bath time, breakfast
pool.explain: Three groups are easier to hold than six things, and each group reminds you what is in it.

pool.prompt: What hidden words make up SUNHATBED?
pool.hint: Look for chunks that are real words.
pool.explain: Sun, hat and bed are real words. Chunks that mean something are the easiest to remember.

pool.prompt: About how many pieces can your memory hold at once?
pool.hint: In the lab, how many numbers fitted in the box?
pool.explain: Your memory holds only a few pieces at once, about 4. That is why chunks help.

pool.prompt: A row of letters hides {w} words, and each word has 3 letters. How many letters are in the row?
pool.hint: Each word is 3 letters. Count 3 for each of the {w} words.
pool.explain: {w} words of 3 letters is {=w*3} letters, but only {w} chunks to remember.

pool.prompt: Which is the best way to chunk 07123456?
pool.hint: Not too many pieces, and none too big.
pool.explain: 0712 3456 is 2 chunks of 4. Single digits make 8 pieces, and one giant chunk is too big.

pool.prompt: Sam chunks 9 numbers like this: 35829 4 7 1 6. What went wrong?
choices: One chunk is too big and the rest are single pieces
pool.hint: Look at the size of each chunk.
pool.explain: 35829 is too big to hold as one, and 4, 7, 1, 6 are 4 extra single pieces. Groups of 3 work better.

pool.prompt: How would you chunk the word remember to spell it?
pool.hint: Clap the beats as you say it slowly.
pool.explain: Remember has 3 beats: re, mem, ber. One beat at a time is easy to spell.

pool.prompt: You hold {a} number chunks and {b} word chunks in your memory. How many chunks is that?
pool.hint: Add the number chunks and the word chunks together.
pool.explain: {a} add {b} is {=a+b} chunks. More than about 4 and some start to fall out.
